title: Reliable Chain-of-Thought via Prefix Consistency
claim: Weighting votes by how often an answer survives regeneration from a truncated prefix reaches majority-voting accuracy with far fewer tokens.
layout: 2 rows: two accuracy-vs-cost plots on top, two mirrored example panels below
description: The top row has two line plots. Each plots accuracy (%) against tokens per problem on a log scale, for GPT-OSS-120B on FrontierScience-Olympiad and Ministral3-14B on AIME 2025. A thick green curve for prefix consistency (ours) rises above black standard majority voting and the blue, orange, red and pink baselines. Dotted lines and callouts mark a near-plateau target. Green headings state '21.7× fewer tokens' and '20.9× fewer tokens'. A shared legend sits beneath the plots. The bottom row has two mirrored panels. The left panel, green, shows a consistent trace whose gold and original answers are both 42. The right panel, red, shows an inconsistent trace whose original answer is 17 and gold answer is 42. Each panel runs through three numbered steps: truncate the original trace at its mid-point, regenerate five continuations from the prefix, and compute prefix consistency. The scores are 5/5 and 2/5. The eye goes first to the green curves, then to the green and red panels.
caption: Overview of prefix consistency. Top: cost-equivalent accuracy of majority voting weighted by prefix consistency and baseline methods on two models and benchmark settings. Shaded bands and error bars show $\pm 2\times$ the Monte Carlo standard error. Bottom: Overview of our proposed method (prefix consistency). Correct reasoning traces exhibit greater reproducibility under regeneration.
abstract: Large language models often improve accuracy on reasoning tasks by sampling multiple chain-of-thought (CoT) traces and aggregating them with majority voting, a test-time technique called self-consistency. When we truncate a CoT partway through and regenerate the remainder, we observe that traces with correct answers reproduce their original answer more often than traces with wrong answers. We use this difference as a reliability signal, prefix consistency, that weights each candidate answer by how often it reappears under regeneration. It requires no access to token log-probabilities or self-rating prompts. Across five reasoning models and four math and science benchmarks, prefix consistency is the best correctness predictor in most settings, and reweighting votes by this signal reaches the plateau accuracy of majority voting with up to $21\times$ fewer tokens (median $4.6\times$). Our code is available at https://github.com/naoto-iwase/prefix-consistency.
